title: Formulas, Functions and Charts
summary: Formulas calculate results from worksheet data and update automatically when the data changes. Elements of a formula: it must begin with the equal to (=) sign; mathematical operators (+ − * /) and logical operators (<, >); cell references (including named ranges); text or values; worksheet functions such as SUM or AVERAGE. The cell shows the result; the formula itself appears in the formula bar when the cell is selected. The Formulas tab holds the function library.
Example: in F3 type =B3+C3+D3+E3 to add four subjects' marks. If A1=2, B1=3, C1=4, D1=5: =B1*C1 gives 12; =A1*B1−C1+D1 gives 7; =((A1*B1)+C1)/D1 gives 2.

Copying a formula: drag the fill handle (small square at the bottom-right of the cell) down or across; the formula is copied and its cell references adjust to each row (relative references). Copying formulas saves time and reduces errors. A $ sign (e.g. $A$1) makes a reference absolute so it does not change when copied.
AutoSum: click the cell, Formulas (or Home) tab → AutoSum → Sum → Enter; or type =SUM(B3:E3).

Functions are built-in formulas; you give the cell references (arguments) inside parentheses. SUM(number1, number2, …) adds numbers (up to 255 arguments); a range is written with a colon, e.g. =SUM(A10:A20). SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) adds only the cells that meet a condition, such as ">99"; blank and text values are ignored. AVERAGE() returns the arithmetic mean; MIN() returns the smallest value; MAX() returns the largest value. COUNT() counts cells containing numbers; COUNTA() counts non-empty cells; COUNTBLANK() counts empty cells; COUNTIF() counts cells meeting a condition. More functions: AutoSum → More Functions (Insert Function dialog).

Charts present worksheet data visually; a chart is a visual representation of data. Types: Column — compares values across categories; Line — shows trends over time at equal intervals; Pie — shows the proportion of each part to the whole; only one data series and preferably 5–6 slices, all positive; Bar — compares individual items (horizontal bars); Area — highlights the degree of change over time and the total value; XY (Scatter) — both axes show values; shows the relationship between two variables; Stock — shows fluctuations in stock prices (High-Low-Close) or temperatures; Surface — finds optimum combinations between two sets of numeric data, coloured like a topographic map; Doughnut — like a pie (parts of a whole) but can have more than one series; Bubble — x values, y values and bubble sizes; Radar — compares aggregate values of several data series.

Components of a chart: chart title; X-axis and Y-axis titles; X-axis categories (from the first column/row of the data); Y-axis values; data labels (the values plotted); legend (colour, symbol or pattern for each data series); tick marks (show the scaling of the axes); gridlines (lines at major intervals).

Drawing a chart in Excel 2007: (1) enter the data; (2) select the data range; (3) Insert tab → Charts group → choose the chart type; (4) choose the sub-type; (5) Chart Tools → Layout → Chart Title, then type the title; (6) Layout → Axis Titles → Primary Horizontal/Vertical Axis Title. Editing: Layout → Legend (position), Data Labels, Data Table, Gridlines. Resize by dragging the handles (corner handles keep proportion); move by dragging the border. Copy the chart and paste it into Word or PowerPoint. Chart Tools add three tabs: Design, Layout and Format.

AutoShapes (Insert → Illustrations → Shapes): lines, connectors (to join flow-chart elements), basic shapes, block arrows, flowchart shapes, stars and banners, callouts. SmartArt (Insert → SmartArt) is a visual representation of information and ideas; choose a type (List, Process, Cycle, Hierarchy, Relationship…) and a layout, then type the text; the Design tab applies effects. Clip Art (Insert → Clip Art) inserts a media file — picture, sound, animation or movie. Picture from file: Insert → Picture → choose the file → Insert; the Format tab (Adjust, Picture Styles, Arrange, Size) edits it.

vsa: Differentiate between the MIN() and MAX() functions.

MIN() returns the smallest number in a set of values, e.g. =MIN(B2:B6) gives the lowest mark. MAX() returns the largest number, e.g. =MAX(B2:B6) gives the highest mark. Both accept up to 255 arguments.
October 2019
What is the SUMIF() function? Give its syntax.

SUMIF adds only those cells that meet a given condition. Syntax: SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range). Example: =SUMIF(B3:E3, ">99") adds only the values greater than 99; blank and text cells are ignored.
April 2023
Differentiate between formulas and functions.

A formula is an expression written by the user, starting with =, using operators and cell references, e.g. =B3+C3+D3. A function is a built-in formula with a name, to which you give arguments in parentheses, e.g. =SUM(B3:D3) or =AVERAGE(B3:D3).
April 2017
What are the elements of a formula in an Excel spreadsheet?

A formula must begin with the = sign and can contain mathematical operators (+, −, *, /) and logical operators (<, >), cell references (including named ranges), text or values, and worksheet functions such as SUM and AVERAGE.

What is a legend in a chart?

Differentiate between AutoShapes and SmartArt graphics.

AutoShapes are ready-made shapes — lines, arrows, basic shapes, flowchart symbols, stars and callouts — drawn one by one. SmartArt creates a complete diagram of ideas, such as a process or hierarchy, from a chosen layout into which text is typed.

Differentiate between a bar chart and an area chart.

A bar chart uses horizontal bars to compare individual items. An area chart plots data as a filled area to highlight the degree of change over time and draw attention to the total value across a trend.

sa: Explain any five components of a chart.

(1) Chart title — the title of the whole chart. (2) Axis titles — names of the X-axis and Y-axis data. (3) X-axis categories and Y-axis values — the categories plotted and the value scale. (4) Legend — colour or pattern used for each data series. (5) Data labels — the values of the data plotted. Also tick marks (scale of axes) and gridlines (lines at major intervals).
Write the steps to plot a pie chart with the title 'First Quarter Sales' for given sales data.

(1) Enter the item names in column A and sales percentages in column B. (2) Select the data range A1:B6. (3) Insert tab → Charts group → Pie → choose a sub-type (2-D Pie). (4) Click the chart → Chart Tools Layout → Chart Title → Above Chart. (5) Type 'First Quarter Sales'. (6) Add data labels from Layout → Data Labels if needed.
A table shows marks in 5 subjects. Write the steps to create a line chart titled 'Performance Analysis' with X-axis 'Subject' and Y-axis 'Score'.

(1) Enter subjects in column A and marks in column B; select the range. (2) Insert → Charts → Line → choose a sub-type. (3) Layout → Chart Title → type 'Performance Analysis'. (4) Layout → Axis Titles → Primary Horizontal Axis Title → type 'Subject'. (5) Layout → Axis Titles → Primary Vertical Axis Title → type 'Score'.

la: What is a chart? Explain any four types of charts available in Excel.

A chart is a visual representation of worksheet data that makes comparisons and trends easy to see. (1) Column chart — vertical bars compare values across categories. (2) Line chart — shows trends over equal intervals of time. (3) Pie chart — shows the proportion of each part to the whole; one data series, best with 5–6 slices. (4) Bar chart — horizontal bars compare individual items. Others: Area (change over time and total), XY Scatter (relationship between two variables), Stock (price fluctuations), Surface, Doughnut, Bubble and Radar.

or: Write the steps to draw a chart in Excel 2007 and give it titles.

(1) Enter the data in the worksheet. (2) Select the data range with the mouse. (3) Insert tab → Charts group → choose a chart type. (4) Choose the sub-type; the chart appears. (5) Click the chart → Chart Tools Layout → Chart Title → type a title. (6) Layout → Axis Titles → Primary Horizontal Axis Title and Primary Vertical Axis Title → type them. (7) Use Legend, Data Labels and Gridlines in the Layout tab to edit; drag handles to resize and the border to move.

la: Explain the SUM, SUMIF, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN and COUNT functions with examples.

SUM adds numbers: =SUM(B2:B6). SUMIF adds cells meeting a condition: =SUMIF(B2:B6, ">50"). AVERAGE gives the arithmetic mean: =AVERAGE(B2:B6). MAX gives the largest value: =MAX(B2:B6). MIN gives the smallest value: =MIN(B2:B6). COUNT counts cells with numbers: =COUNT(B2:B6) (COUNTA counts non-empty cells, COUNTBLANK empty ones, COUNTIF cells meeting a condition). Each function takes up to 255 arguments, written in parentheses after the name, starting with =.
